Senses.Explanation: In the Chan records the ordinary monastic water-vessel is repurposed as a naming-and-checking test-object: the named Chan figure forbids calling the bottle by its own name and demands a different response, and knocking it over settles a succession contest. In the Baizhang–Guishan encounter Baizhang points to the bottle and asks what it should be called if it may not be called a clean-water bottle (不得喚作淨瓶); the head cook Guishan answers not in words but by knocking it over (蹋倒淨瓶), and is thereby recorded as the successor. That test-object deployment — who sets the test and what the kick decides — is the word's Zen bend. Literally a ‘clean bottle,’ this is a bottle used for water. The allowlisted corpus has 487 hits in 143 texts. Recorded actions establish the object without requiring an imported technical gloss: a named record subject asks for the bottle to be passed and then returned to its former place; another calls an attendant and says, ‘Add water to the clean-water bottle’; Guishan passes one to Yangshan and draws it back before Yangshan can receive it; and one biography reports water surging from a bottle. It is also the object in the Baizhang–Guishan case: Baizhang points to it and asks what it should be called if it may not be called a clean-water bottle, after which Guishan knocks it over. Later collections title and repeatedly comment on this case. The word continues to name the concrete bottle throughout those exchanges.
Senses.Note: The Zen bend is institutional, not a separate lexical sense: the ordinary water-vessel becomes the naming-test object whose knocking-over decides a succession (不得喚作淨瓶 … 蹋倒淨瓶). The seven required definition formulas were searched. The corpus does not supply a separate lexical equation, but it repeatedly identifies the object through passing, filling, returning, tipping, and knocking it over. The failed draft candidate from the Tianyin record was excluded because its proposed span did not pass exact verification; no unverified text was retained.
